paragraphs.source_en: At around 7,500 BP the Pastoral economy based on domesticated cattle is attested to across the Central Sahara. The first domestication took place probably in the Eastern Sahara in the area of Nabta Playa and Bir Kiseiba (Smith 1992; Hassan 2002). From this nuclear area, the keeping of cattle with the new populations spread to the Central Sahara. Not only were the style, dimensions and themes of the Pastoral rock art different from the Round Head paintings thus indicating people of a different culture, but a population replacement at around 7,200 BP is also attested to in the Gobero cemetery in Niger. The introduction of new groups and herds to the territory occupied by local hunter-gatherers may have caused a variety of reactions or relationships.

paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the rock art, no scene of fighting between individuals or groups is known in the Round Head art; their themes remained peaceful and highly symbolical. The relationship of the herders towards the Round Head art is perceptible from the Pastoral paintings. The themes of the Pastoral art mainly consist of herds of domesticated cattle associated with men and women, everyday life scenes and occasionally hunting scenes of mouflon. Their paintings are found in a much larger geographical area exceeding the borders of the Round Head territory. In the Tassili, Algerian Tadrart and in the Acacus Pastoral paintings are located both in empty shelters, previously not used, and also in shelters where Round Head paintings were already present.

paragraphs.source_en: During my fieldwork I examined hundreds of Round Head paintings and I noticed that very few of them, given the total number, are actually superimposed by the later Pastoral paintings. When the Pastoral figures are present on the same wall, they are often placed next to the Round Head figures which are usually always in the central part of the wall, whereas the Pastoral paintings are on its borders. Round Head figures never appear damaged by later paintings or intentionally destroyed, on the contrary, when figures of domesticated cattle are painted in the same panels as the Round Heads, they rather seem to fill in the empty spaces of the wall between the Round Head figures. A sign of respect for the previous Round Head art is therefore evident from the position of the Pastoral paintings when placed on the same wall.
